
z3r connects R to [Z3](https://github.com/Z3Prover/z3), a satisfiability
modulo theories (SMT) solver. You describe a problem as logical constraints
over integers, exact reals, Booleans, bit-vectors, arrays, strings and
functions; Z3 either finds values that satisfy all of them, proves that none
exist, or reports that it could not decide.

z3r is an independent third-party package. It is not developed or endorsed by
Microsoft or by the Z3 team.

```{r}
library(z3r)
z3_version()$runtime
```

## What an SMT solver does

An SMT solver answers one question: *is there an assignment of values to
these variables that makes all of these formulas true?* The answer is

* `"sat"`: yes, and here is one (a *model*);
* `"unsat"`: no, provably not;
* `"unknown"`: Z3 gave up. This happens with resource limits, and with
  theories for which no complete algorithm exists (nonlinear integer
  arithmetic, quantifiers). `"unknown"` never means `"unsat"`.

This differs from tools R users know:

| Tool | Works with | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `optim()`, `nloptr` | continuous functions, floating point | a local optimum, approximately |
| linear/integer programming (`lpSolve`, `ompr`) | linear constraints | a global optimum |
| computer algebra (SymPy, `symcompR`, `Ryacas`) | symbolic expressions | closed-form solutions, simplifications |
| SMT (Z3) | arbitrary logical combinations of constraints in many theories | a model, a proof of impossibility, or "unknown" |

An SMT solver is the right tool when the problem is *combinatorial* or
*logical*: disjunctions ("this job runs before that one, or after it"),
implications, integer and bit-level reasoning, and questions of the form
"does this hold for **all** inputs?". Numbers are exact: integers have
unbounded size and reals are rationals or algebraic numbers, never rounded
floating point.

## A first problem

```{r}
ctx <- z3_context()
x <- z3_int(ctx, "x")
y <- z3_int(ctx, "y")

s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, x + y == 10, x > 2 * y, y > 0)
z3_check(s)
m <- z3_model(s)
m
z3_value(z3_eval(m, x))
```

The three objects are always the same: a **context** owns everything, a
**solver** collects constraints, and a **model** holds the values found by
the last satisfiable check.

Constraints are built with ordinary R operators. They do not compute
anything; they build formulas:

```{r}
x + y == 10
x^2 + y^2 <= 25
```

R's `&&` and `||` cannot be overloaded, so use `&`, `|`, `!` or the
functions `z3_and()`, `z3_or()`, `z3_not()`, `z3_implies()`:

```{r}
p <- z3_bool(ctx, "p")
z3_implies(p, x > 0) & (p | y < 0)
```

A formula is never silently converted to `TRUE` or `FALSE`, so mistakes such
as `if (x > 0)` are errors rather than wrong answers:

```{r, error = TRUE}
if (x > 0) "positive"
```

## Exact numbers

Z3 integers are unbounded and Z3 reals are exact, so z3r never passes values
through double precision unless asked to:

```{r}
big <- z3_int_val(ctx, "123456789012345678901234567890")
z3_simplify(big * big)
z3_real_val(ctx, "1/3") + z3_real_val(ctx, "1/6")
z3_simplify(z3_real_val(ctx, "1/3") + z3_real_val(ctx, "1/6"))
```

R numbers mixed with formulas are converted by a documented rule (see
`?z3_int_val`): whole numbers become exact integers, and `0.1` becomes the
rational 1/10, which is the number R prints, not the binary approximation
R stores. Whole numbers beyond 2^53 are refused, because R may already have
rounded them; pass such numbers as strings or `gmp::bigz`.

Converting results back to R is exact as well. `z3_value()` returns a double
only when the value is exactly representable, and otherwise a `gmp` number
(or a string when gmp is not installed):

```{r}
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
r <- z3_real(ctx, "r")
z3_add(s, x == z3_int_val(ctx, "1180591620717411303424"), 3 * r == 1)
z3_check(s)
z3_model_values(z3_model(s))
```

Division follows R: `/` is real division even for integers. `%/%` and `%%`
are Z3's integer `div` and `mod`, which use the SMT-LIB (Euclidean)
convention. It agrees with R for positive divisors and differs for negative
ones:

```{r}
z3_simplify(z3_int_val(ctx, 7) %/% -2)
7 %/% -2
```

## Nonlinear problems and algebraic numbers

Z3 decides nonlinear real arithmetic exactly. Irrational solutions are
algebraic numbers:

```{r}
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, r * r == 2, r > 0)
z3_check(s)
root <- z3_eval(z3_model(s), r)
root
z3_decimal(root, 20)
z3_value(root, exact = FALSE)
```

Nonlinear *integer* arithmetic is undecidable in general, so Z3 may answer
`"unknown"` or run for a long time. Limits keep checks bounded:

```{r}
z <- z3_int(ctx, "z")
s <- z3_solver(ctx, timeout = 500)
z3_add(s, x > 0, y > 0, z > 0, x^3 + y^3 == z^3)
z3_check(s)
z3_reason_unknown(s)
```

Use `rlimit` instead of `timeout` for results that are reproducible across
machines. Ctrl-C also stops a running check.

## Proving things for all inputs

To prove that a formula is always true, ask whether its negation can be
satisfied. `"unsat"` is a proof.

```{r}
a <- z3_int(ctx, "a")
b <- z3_int(ctx, "b")
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, !(z3_abs(a + b) <= z3_abs(a) + z3_abs(b)))
z3_check(s)
```

The triangle inequality holds for every pair of (unbounded) integers. No
amount of random testing gives that guarantee.

## A realistic example: scheduling with disjunctions

Three jobs share one machine. Each has a duration and a release time; job 2
must finish before job 3 starts. We want the earliest time at which all jobs
are done. The "no overlap" requirement is a disjunction for every pair, so
the feasible region is not convex, and gradient-based optimizers such as
`optim()` have nothing to follow; integer programming needs big-M
reformulations. For an SMT optimizer it is the natural formulation.

```{r}
dur <- c(4, 3, 2)
release <- c(0, 1, 5)
start <- z3_ints(ctx, paste0("start", 1:3))

opt <- z3_optimize(ctx)
for (i in 1:3) z3_add(opt, start[[i]] >= release[i])
for (i in 1:2) for (j in (i + 1):3) {
  z3_add(opt, start[[i]] + dur[i] <= start[[j]] | start[[j]] + dur[j] <= start[[i]])
}
z3_add(opt, start[[2]] + dur[2] <= start[[3]])
makespan <- z3_int(ctx, "makespan")
for (i in 1:3) z3_add(opt, makespan >= start[[i]] + dur[i])
obj <- z3_minimize(opt, makespan)

z3_check(opt)
z3_optimum(obj)
unlist(z3_model_values(z3_model(opt))[paste0("start", 1:3)])
```

The answer is optimal: Z3 proves no schedule finishes earlier.

## Incremental solving

A solver keeps its assertions between checks. `z3_push()` and `z3_pop()`
open and close scopes, which is how "what if" questions are asked without
rebuilding the problem:

```{r}
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, x > 0, x < 10)
z3_push(s)
z3_add(s, x > 20)
z3_check(s)
z3_pop(s)
z3_check(s)
```

Assumptions hold for a single check only:

```{r}
z3_check(s, x == 5)
z3_check(s, x == 50)
```

A model is only handed out for the check that produced it. After the solver
changes, `z3_model()` refuses until the next `z3_check()`, so a model never
describes constraints it was not computed for.

## Explaining contradictions: unsatisfiable cores

Label constraints with `z3_assert_and_track()`. When the problem is
unsatisfiable, `z3_unsat_core()` names a subset of the labels that is already
contradictory:

```{r}
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_assert_and_track(s, x > 10, "at_least_11")
z3_assert_and_track(s, x < 5, "at_most_4")
z3_assert_and_track(s, x != 7, "not_seven")
z3_check(s)
names(z3_unsat_core(s))
```

Cores are not guaranteed to be minimal.

## Optimization with soft constraints

Soft constraints are preferences with weights. The optimizer minimizes the
total weight of the preferences it has to give up:

```{r}
want <- z3_bools(ctx, c("coffee", "tea", "juice"))
opt <- z3_optimize(ctx)
z3_add(opt, z3_or(!want$coffee, !want$tea))     # not both hot drinks
z3_add(opt, z3_or(!want$tea, !want$juice))
z3_add_soft(opt, want$coffee, 2)
z3_add_soft(opt, want$tea, 3)
z3_add_soft(opt, want$juice, 2)
z3_check(opt)
unlist(z3_model_values(z3_model(opt)))
```

Optimal values are not always attained or finite; `z3_optimum()` reports
`"unbounded"` and `"not attained"` (an infimum or supremum approached with
an infinitesimal `epsilon`) instead of inventing a number:

```{r}
opt <- z3_optimize(ctx)
z3_add(opt, r < 3)
z3_optimum({
  h <- z3_maximize(opt, r)
  z3_check(opt)
  h
})
```
